data-scan.name: Data scan
data-scan.navDesc: One week, and you know where you stand
data-scan.recognise: You know there's more in your data than you're getting out of it, but not where to start — and every proposal you get opens with a three-month engagement.
data-scan.promise: In one week you know exactly where you stand and what to do first.
deliverables: An inventory of every data source and what's actually in it
A maturity score, so you know where you stand
A prioritised roadmap for the next twelve months
2–3 quick wins you can implement yourself
data-scan.intro: The data scan is the fastest way to learn what to do first — and the cheapest way to find out whether we're a fit. One week, a fixed price, and at the end a document you can act on with or without me.

steps.label: Day 1 — Conversations
steps.body: I talk to the people who work with the data and the people who steer on it. What gets asked for, what can't be answered, where the time goes.

steps.label: Day 2–3 — Into the systems
steps.body: I look inside your sources myself: what's in there, how clean it is, how it fits together. No assumptions based on what should be there.

steps.label: Day 4 — Working it out
steps.body: The maturity score, the bottlenecks ranked by impact, and per step an estimate of what it costs and what it returns.

steps.label: Day 5 — Delivery
steps.body: A presentation to your team, the roadmap on the table, and the quick wins you can still implement yourself this month.

requirements-and-kpis.name: Sharpen the question
requirements-and-kpis.navDesc: Know what you're building, before you build
requirements-and-kpis.recognise: There's budget for a dashboard or a system, but the question behind it isn't written down anywhere — and everyone means something different by 'active customer'.
requirements-and-kpis.promise: A specification that can be built from directly, and one definition per figure that everyone stands behind.
deliverables: One definition per KPI, with an owner attached
A measurability check: is what you're asking for even in your data?
Acceptance criteria — when is it done and right
An explicit list of what is not included
A build estimate, usable by me or by someone else
requirements-and-kpis.intro: The cheapest way to avoid building the wrong thing. At the end you have a specification that can be built from directly, definitions everyone stands behind, and the certainty that your data can actually fill them. Including if you then have someone else build it — the brief is yours, not mine.

steps.label: Day 1–2 — Collecting the question
steps.body: I talk to the people who'll use it and the person paying for it. Which decision do you need to be able to make, and what happens today when you can't.

steps.label: Day 3–4 — Pinning down definitions
steps.body: One definition per figure, with an owner. What counts, what doesn't, and who decides when it's contested.

steps.label: Week 2 — Measurability check
steps.body: I look inside your sources myself to see whether what's being asked for can be produced. A KPI nobody can populate isn't a KPI, and you'd rather hear that now than after the build.

steps.label: Delivery — The brief
steps.body: Acceptance criteria, the scope with an explicit list of what falls outside it, and a build estimate. Ready to put out to tender or pick up yourself.

dashboards.name: A dashboard people actually open
dashboards.navDesc: Reporting on the source you already have
dashboards.recognise: There's a dashboard. Nobody opens it. Or: the data sits in your system, but 'how are we doing' still means calling Finance.
dashboards.promise: Dashboards built around the decisions your team actually makes — on the source you already have.
deliverables: An inventory of the decisions that come back every month
A clean data model on your existing source
1–3 dashboards with drill-down into the detail
A definition list, so every figure traces back
An adoption session with the users — not a manual by email
dashboards.intro: For when your data already sits somewhere usable and you mostly want something to finally come out of it that people look at. No warehouse project needed: I build on the source you have. Most dashboards don't die on technology, they die on use — so the adoption session is in scope by default.

steps.label: Week 1 — Mapping the decisions
steps.body: Not 'which chart do you want' but 'which decision do you make again every month'. The dashboard gets built around that.

steps.label: Week 1–2 — Model on your source
steps.body: A clean data model on what you already have, with one definition per figure. No warehouse project required.

steps.label: Week 2–3 — Build and sharpen
steps.body: The dashboards, with drill-down into the detail the questions are about. You look along as it goes — no single big reveal at the end.

steps.label: Closing — Adoption
steps.body: A session with the people who'll use it, in their own calendar. A manual by email doesn't work.

single-source-of-truth.name: One version of the truth
single-source-of-truth.navDesc: One data warehouse, one definition per figure
single-source-of-truth.recognise: Three departments, three revenue figures, and every monthly meeting opens with an argument about whose number is right.
single-source-of-truth.promise: One data warehouse that all your reporting runs on — and no more arguments about whose figure is right.
deliverables: A modelled data warehouse on your own sources
Tested transformations with daily data-quality checks
A Power BI dashboard on your KPIs
Documentation that pins down every definition
A handover session with your team
single-source-of-truth.bridge: Built so you can put AI on top of it later — no rebuild needed.
single-source-of-truth.intro: This is the work I'm most at home in: from scattered sources to one modelled data warehouse, with reporting on top that people actually trust. Everything in version control, everything tested, everything documented — so your team takes it over instead of depending on me.

steps.label: Week 1 — Model
steps.body: We pin down the definitions: what counts as a customer, when an order counts, which KPIs you actually steer on. That becomes the data model.

steps.label: Week 2 — Build
steps.body: Pipelines on your sources, transformations with a test at every step, and a warehouse that's ready every morning.

steps.label: Week 3 — Dashboard
steps.body: The dashboard on your KPIs, with drill-down into the detail the questions are really about.

steps.label: Week 4 — Handover
steps.body: Documentation, a session with your team, and the keys. From here you carry on yourselves.

reporting-automation.name: Reporting on autopilot
reporting-automation.recognise: The same two days every month: pull the exports, paste into Excel, re-check the figures, and hope nothing slipped.
reporting-automation.promise: That monthly report costing two days of manual work? From now on it runs itself.
deliverables: An automated pipeline on your existing sources
The report in your inbox or dashboard, on schedule
An alert the moment something breaks — before your stakeholders notice
Handover, so you can change it yourself
reporting-automation.bridge: Built so you can put AI on top of it later — no rebuild needed.
reporting-automation.intro: The smallest package, and often the one that pays back fastest. One report that's manual today becomes a pipeline that runs itself — including an alert when something goes wrong.

steps.label: Day 1–2 — Unpicking it
steps.body: We walk through the report step by step the way you make it now. Every action, including the small corrections nobody writes down.

steps.label: Week 1 — Build
steps.body: The steps become code: fetch, validate, calculate, publish. With tests exactly where it goes wrong today.

steps.label: Week 2 — Live and handover
steps.body: The pipeline runs on schedule, the report arrives, and you know how to adjust it when a column is added.

ai-prototype.name: AI prototype in 3 weeks
ai-prototype.navDesc: A working prototype and an honest verdict
ai-prototype.recognise: There's an AI idea on the table. Nobody can say whether it works, what it costs, or whether it's worth doing.
ai-prototype.promise: From AI idea to working prototype — including an honest verdict on whether it should go ahead.
deliverables: One use case built out into working software
Measured quality against a real test set — not a gut feeling
Cost per user per month, worked out
A go/no-go recommendation — including when that's 'don't'
ai-prototype.intro: Three weeks, one use case, and an honest answer at the end. I build the prototype for real — working software, not a clickable mockup — and measure whether it's good enough. If it isn't, I'll say so. For a fixed price you'll have avoided sinking a year into it.

steps.label: Week 1 — Scope and yardstick
steps.body: One use case, tightly scoped. And up front: when is it good enough? We build that test set before the first line of code.

steps.label: Week 2 — Building
steps.body: Working software on your data, in your own environment. With citations, so every answer traces back to its source.

steps.label: Week 3 — Measure and judge
steps.body: Quality against the test set, cost per user per month worked out, and a go/no-go with the reasoning attached.

ai-workshop.name: AI literacy for your team
ai-workshop.navDesc: One day, your whole team up to speed
ai-workshop.recognise: Your team is already using AI, except nobody is quite sure what it can do, what it can't, and what's allowed with company data.
ai-workshop.promise: After one day your team knows what AI can and can't do — and where it actually pays off in your work.
deliverables: A day on site, tailored to the work you actually do
Hands-on exercises with your own documents and processes
Clear ground rules on what is and isn't allowed (GDPR and the AI Act)
A prioritised list of use cases your team came up with themselves
ai-workshop.intro: A day with your team, on site. No slides about how AI is changing the world — hands-on work with your own documents and processes, and clear ground rules by the end.

steps.label: Morning — What it is
steps.body: How a language model works, why it sometimes produces confident nonsense, and how to spot it. In plain language.

steps.label: Afternoon — Hands on
steps.body: Working with your own documents and processes. Everyone builds something that works.

steps.label: Closing — Ground rules and next steps
steps.body: What is and isn't allowed with company data, and a prioritised list of use cases your team came up with themselves.

home.metaDescription: I build data foundations that carry both your reporting and your AI. Five packages with fixed scope, fixed price and a timeline in weeks.

hero.title: You have data and AI plans. What's missing in between is the foundation.
hero.subtitle: I build data foundations that carry both your reporting and your AI. Fixed scope, fixed price, in weeks — not quarters.

problem.title: Where it actually breaks down
problem.card1Title: Every department has a different number
problem.card1Body: Revenue from the CRM doesn't match revenue from the books, and nobody knows which of the two you show the bank.
problem.card2Body: Two days of exporting, pasting and re-checking. Every month again — and one formula dragged one row too far goes unnoticed for months.
problem.card3Title: The AI plan is hanging in mid-air
problem.card3Body: There's an idea and there's budget, but nobody can say whether the data it needs is usable in the first place.
problem.closer: All three have the same cause: there's no foundation underneath. That's what I build.

services.title: The foundation first. Then the AI on top actually works.
services.subtitle: Most AI projects fail on the data, not the model. I build the layer underneath — and it's exactly the same layer your reporting runs on.
services.service1Body: From scattered spreadsheets to a reliable data foundation with dashboards that actually answer questions.
services.service2Body: Practical AI solutions: document processing, RAG systems, automations, and AI strategy that works.

packages.title: Fixed scope, fixed price
packages.subtitle: No billing by the hour but defined packages, each with a fixed timeline and a concrete result. Not sure which one fits? Start with the data scan.

process.title: From first conversation to working solution
process.step1Body: I map where you stand with data and AI, and where the opportunities are.
process.step2Body: Based on the scan we draw up a concrete plan with priorities and quick wins.
process.step3Body: I build the solution: data pipelines, dashboards, AI tools, automations.
process.step4Body: I train your team, document everything, and make sure you can run it yourselves.

whyFreelance.title: Senior capability, no overhead
whyFreelance.subtitle: One person doing the work himself, with a background you don't buy off a staffing shelf.
whyFreelance.card1Body: You buy a result with an agreed scope and a fixed price. If it runs over, that's my risk — which is how an engagement should work.
whyFreelance.card2Body: At the police and in aerospace you work under hard privacy and information-security requirements. Privacy by design isn't an appendix to my proposal.
whyFreelance.card3Body: Since 2020 I've explained complex technology on Udemy to thousands of people without a technical background. I do the same at handover to your team.
whyFreelance.card4Title: I build myself out of the picture
whyFreelance.card4Body: Documentation, tests and a handover session are part of every engagement. The goal is that you don't need me afterwards.

ai.title: GenAI built like serious software
ai.sub: No black box that disappears into a drawer after the pilot. I treat AI solutions as serious software: evaluated, documented and under version control — so your team takes over effortlessly after I leave.
ai.f1Body: Test sets and LangFuse tracing from day one: measuring quality instead of hoping for the best.
ai.f2Body: Prompts, pipelines and infrastructure in version control — reviewable, reproducible and transferable.
ai.f3Body: Source references by default: from answer back to the underlying document. No black box.
ai.f4Body: Everything runs in your own cloud tenant. Privacy by design, GDPR and AI Act proof.

analytics.title: Analytics built like serious software
analytics.sub: No sprawl of loose scripts and manual exports. I treat data pipelines as serious software: tested, documented and under version control — so your team can carry on without me.
analytics.f1Body: Validation and quality checks at every pipeline step: errors surface before they reach your dashboard.
analytics.f2Body: Transformations, data models and infrastructure in version control — reviewable, reproducible and transferable.
analytics.f3Body: One definition per KPI, from dashboard back to the source — no more arguing over whose number is right.
analytics.f4Body: Everything runs in your own environment. Privacy by design and GDPR-proof.

items: Bespoke data engineering — pipelines, warehousing and integrations outside a package
Ad-hoc analysis — one sharp question about pricing, churn or funnel, investigated and evidenced

proof.title: Why you'd take this from me
proof.subtitle: I've done data work in aerospace and at the police, where a wrong figure has real consequences. And since 2020 I've been explaining complex technology on Udemy to thousands of people without a technical background — which is most of what this job is.

items.q: Why a fixed price instead of an hourly rate?
items.a: Because you're buying a result, not hours. Scope and price are on paper up front; if it runs over, that's my problem and not yours. Work outside the packages runs on a day rate — I'll name it in the first conversation.

A short introductory call first. Then a proposal with scope, schedule and price on a single page. During the work you get a short weekly update and working software to look at — no status report at the end. We close with documentation and a handover session.

items.q: Do you work on site or remotely?
items.a: Both. I work out of Noord-Holland and am happy to come in for the kick-off, the interim sessions and the handover. The building itself I do remotely — it's faster that way.

items.q: What kind of contract do we sign?
items.a: A contract for services with an obligation of result: defined scope, fixed price, clear delivery. I'm used to working for clients with their own procurement terms and information-security requirements.

cta.title: Not sure which package fits?
cta.subtitle: Book a free half-hour call. Then you'll know — and you're committed to nothing.

about.metaTitle: About me — data engineer at NLR and the Dutch police
about.metaDescription: Data and AI consultant with a background at NLR and the Dutch police, and thousands of students on Udemy. I build data foundations for reporting and AI.
about.name: Ruud Juffermans
about.intro1: At Politie Noord-Holland I applied data analysis, automation and AI within criminal law — an environment where a wrong figure has real consequences, and where privacy and information security are not an afterthought. Before that I built a wide range of data projects as a data engineer at the Netherlands Aerospace Centre (NLR).
about.intro2: Since 2020 I've published courses on Udemy, by now with thousands of students. Explaining complex technology to people without a technical background is the entire job there — and it's also most of what a client is actually buying from me. A dashboard nobody understands isn't a dashboard.
about.intro3: The same thing came back in both worlds: organisations sitting on valuable data without getting information out of it, making AI plans with no foundation underneath. I started this practice to close that gap — for companies that don't have a twenty-person data team.
about.pullQuote: I've seen what happens when data and AI work — and what happens when they don't.

privacy.metaDescription: Privacy statement of Ruud Juffermans — Data Analytics & AI Consultant.
privacy.title: Privacy statement

sections.title: 1. Who I am
sections.content: Ruud Juffermans, operating as Data Analytics & AI Consultant, based in Noord-Holland, Netherlands. Email: ruudjuffermans@pm.me.

sections.title: 2. What data I collect
sections.content: Via the contact form: name, email address, optional company name and your message. Via the newsletter: email address. I use privacy-friendly analytics (no cookies, no personal data).

sections.title: 3. Why I collect this data
sections.content: To answer your question and contact you. To send the newsletter you signed up for. To improve the website based on anonymized usage statistics.

sections.title: 4. How long I keep data
sections.content: Contact-form data is kept as long as needed to handle your request, up to a maximum of 12 months. Newsletter data is kept until you unsubscribe.

sections.title: 5. Sharing with third parties
sections.content: I don't share your data with third parties, except where needed for service delivery: Proton (email sending) and Buttondown (newsletter). These processors operate under data-processing agreements.

sections.title: 6. Your rights
sections.content: You have the right to access, correct, delete and transfer your data. You can also object to processing. Contact ruudjuffermans@pm.me for any of these. You can also file a complaint with the Dutch Data Protection Authority.

sections.title: 7. Cookies
sections.content: This website doesn't use tracking cookies. No cookie banner is needed.

sections.title: 8. Changes
sections.content: This privacy statement may be updated. The latest version is always available on this page.
